findings.title: No random seeding anywhere — every run is non-reproducible, contradicting the README's determinism claims
findings.description: No random.seed or seed parameter exists anywhere in the codebase (grep-verified), yet randomness drives nearly every decision: starting money randint(100,150) (entities.py:39), agent processing order shuffled every tick and every day-rollover (manager.py:177, 192), destination/adjacent/home spot choice (manager.py:131, 158, 265, 303), interaction durations (manager.py:338), socialize probability gates and partner choice (behavior/agent_behaviors.py:119, 123, 155, 219, 221), and rest-location choice (agent_behaviors.py:454). Combined with the shuffled, order-dependent cross-agent mutation in tick() (F14/F15), no run, bug report, or generated story can ever be reproduced or replayed — none of the quantitative results in README 'Results and Analysis' (lines 315-398) are reproducible, and this directly contradicts README.md:136/142/402, which repeatedly describes agent control as 'deterministic and operates independently of the LLM'. For a system pitched as a research artifact this is a fundamental gap.
findings.fix: Introduce a single seeded RNG (random.Random(seed)) injected from config or a CLI flag into manager/entities/behaviors, log the seed with every run (defaulting to a logged random value), and soften or qualify the README's determinism claims.

verdict.justification: Repo-wide grep finds no random.seed or seed injection in any runtime code; the only 'seed' occurrences are nx.spring_layout(..., seed=42) in narrative_analyzer.py:855 (graph visualization layout only) and docs/v2_upgrade drafts that themselves list 'seeded RNG' as a planned fix, corroborating the gap. All five simulation modules import the module-level random (global RNG seeded from OS entropy): entities.py:4, manager.py:4, config.py:5, agent_behaviors.py:6, behavior_tree.py:6. Every cited call site verified at the exact line: entities.py:39 (money randint(100,150)); manager.py:177 and 192 (random.shuffle of agent processing order on day rollover and every tick, read in context of the tick function); manager.py:131/158/265/303 (direction shuffle, random.choice of destination/adjacent/home spots); manager.py:338 (randint(15,25) interaction duration); agent_behaviors.py:119/123 (random.random() probability gates), 155/219 (random.choice of partner), 221 (randint(8,15)), 454 (random.choice of rest location). The probability gates make agent decisions genuinely stochastic, so even a charitable reading of 'deterministic' as 'rule-based' fails. README contradiction verified: line 132 ('deterministic control of multi-agent behavior... stable and predictable'), line 136 (verbatim 'This process is deterministic and operates independently of the LLM'), line 402 ('Behavior Trees for deterministic agent control... predictable'); a grep of README.md for random/stochastic/reproduc/non-determin returns zero matches, so no qualification exists anywhere. The Results and Analysis section (lines 315-398) presents specific unreproducible quantitative figures (0.149 average similarity, per-agent rankings). Two trivial imprecisions do not rise to PARTIAL: the finding cites README:142 among the determinism lines, but that line says 'logical and physically plausible' while the third 'deterministic' claim is actually at line 132; and full reproducibility of the README metrics would also require LLM determinism, though the finding never claims seeding alone suffices and its fix includes softening the README claims. Severity Major is appropriate for a research artifact whose documentation repeatedly asserts determinism while every behavioral decision draws from an unseeded global RNG.

findings.title: Restarting the simulation silently overwrites previous runs' diaries and stories
findings.description: Diary and story files are keyed only by day number: daily_stories/day_{day_number}/{agent_id}_{day_name}.txt and {day_name}_story.txt, opened with mode 'w' (narrative_system.py:38-42, 67-69). AgentManager always restarts at day_index 0 / Monday (manager.py:50-56) with an empty daily_stories list (manager.py:59), and nothing persists or restores the sim day across runs. Every restart therefore re-generates day_1, day_2, ... and overwrites the previous run's LLM output in place — the only durable artifact the system produces is destroyed, and runs are not comparable. Combined with the crash-on-LLM-error finding (F01), a crash at day N plus a restart wipes the narrative history that motivated the project.
findings.fix: Namespace output under a per-run directory (e.g. daily_stories/run_{timestamp}/day_{n}/) created once in NarrativeSystem.__init__, or persist day_index/state to disk and resume instead of restarting from day 1.

verdict.justification: Every element of the claim checks out in the code. (1) Output paths are keyed solely by day number and deterministic day name: narrative_system.py:9 fixes DAILY_STORY_DIR to simulation/narrative/daily_stories with no run namespacing; diaries are written to day_{day_number}/{agent.id}_{day_name}.txt with mode 'w' (lines 38-42) and the town story to day_{day_number}/{day_name}_story.txt with mode 'w' (lines 67-69). (2) Every process launch starts from scratch: command.py:61 constructs a fresh AgentManager whose __init__ hardcodes 'day_index': 0 / Monday (manager.py:50-56) and daily_stories = [] (manager.py:59); a repo-wide grep finds no pickle/json/save/resume mechanism persisting simulation day state. (3) The 3 AM narrative flush (manager.py:356-366) computes day_number = prev_day_index + 1 and prev_day_name = days[prev_day_index % 7], and agent IDs come from static AGENT_CONFIG, so run N+1 produces byte-identical file paths to run N and mode 'w' truncates the old content — day_1 of the new run silently destroys day_1 of the old run, then day_2, and so on as the new run progresses. (4) These two writes are the only file outputs of the running system (grep for write-mode open() across all .py files), and narrative_analyzer.py:96 consumes exactly this directory as its research corpus, so the overwritten files are indeed the project's durable deliverable. reset_agent_diaries (narrative_system.py:72-75) is a no-op and nothing else guards, archives, or namespaces the directory. The only nuance — the old run's history is overwritten progressively as the new run reaches each day, not wiped instantly at restart — is already how the finding phrases it ('re-generates day_1, day_2, ... and overwrites ... in place'), so the description does not overstate the mechanism. Major severity is appropriate for silent, unrecoverable loss of the system's primary output on every restart.

findings.title: Pause/Resume is permanently disabled in the README's documented startup order
findings.description: The pause button is only enabled by the 'command_client_ready' event (script.js:39-44), which the server broadcasts exactly once, at the moment command.py connects (command.py:20, app.py:53-56). Following README.md:100-113 (start app.py, then command.py, THEN open the browser), the browser connects after that one-shot broadcast and never receives it, so script.js:317 ('dom.pauseBtn.disabled = true' at the end of initialize()) leaves the button disabled forever — the documented Pause/Resume feature is unusable in the normal startup order. There is also a race in the reverse order: if 'command_client_ready' arrives while initialize() is still awaiting fetch('/map_data.json'), the handler enables the button at line 43 and then line 317 re-disables it. The simulation still renders (line 47's guard stays false), masking the breakage.
findings.fix: Track engine-ready state server-side (set a flag when the command client connects/disconnects) and emit it to each newly connected client in app.py's handle_connect; on the frontend, also treat the first 'simulation_state_update' as proof the engine is ready (set isEngineReady=true and enable the button), and set the initial disabled state in the HTML instead of after the async fetch.

verdict.justification: Every element of the claim is verifiable in the code. (1) The pause button is enabled in exactly one place: static/script.js:43, inside the 'command_client_ready' handler (lines 39-44). (2) That event is emitted once by command.py:20 in its connect handler and rebroadcast once by app.py:53-56 to clients connected at that instant; app.py's handle_connect (lines 43-46) only prints and replays no ready state, and Socket.IO does not persist events for late joiners. (3) README.md:100-113 documents the order app.py → command.py → open browser, so the browser connects after the one-shot broadcast, isEngineReady (script.js:8) stays false, and script.js:317 ('dom.pauseBtn.disabled = true' at the end of initialize()) leaves the button disabled with nothing left to re-enable it; the click handler at script.js:272 never fires on a disabled button, making the documented Pause/Resume feature (README.md:50) unusable. (4) The masking claim is correct: script.js:47's guard 'if (isSimulationPaused && isEngineReady) return;' evaluates false (isSimulationPaused=true at line 18, isEngineReady=false), so simulation_state_update events still render agents and the clock, making the UI look healthy. (5) The reverse-order race is also real: socket = io() connects at script parse (line 35) while initialize() awaits fetch('/map_data.json') (line 292), so a 'command_client_ready' arriving during the await is enabled at line 43 and then re-disabled at line 317 — though this window is narrow and the typical browser-first order works. Minor additional nuance not in the claim (does not change the verdict): index.html:31 ships the button without a disabled attribute, so it is briefly clickable before line 317 runs. Severity Major is appropriate: a documented UI feature is permanently broken under the documented workflow, but the core simulation and visualization remain functional.

findings.title: updateAgentAvatar dereferences null on every agent's first state update — a TypeError on each page load aborts the tick handler
findings.description: script.js:137-139: `let agentDiv = document.getElementById(...); if (!agentDiv) createAgentAvatar(agent); agentDiv.style.left = ...`. createAgentAvatar appends the new div but returns nothing and agentDiv is never reassigned, so on the first update for each agent `agentDiv.style.left` throws 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of null'. The throw aborts the serverAgents.forEach inside the 'simulation_state_update' handler (script.js:59-63), so the remaining agents are not processed and renderAgentSelectionPanel/inspector refresh (lines 64-67) are skipped that tick. With N agents the page throws N uncaught exceptions and takes N ticks (~0.4s each) for all avatars and the roster to appear; the same throw recurs any time a new agent appears mid-run.
findings.fix: Make createAgentAvatar return the created element and write `if (!agentDiv) agentDiv = createAgentAvatar(agent);` (or re-fetch with getElementById after creation).

verdict.justification: static/script.js:137-139 behaves exactly as claimed: `agentDiv` is null on an agent's first update, `createAgentAvatar(agent)` (lines 116-134) appends the div via `dom.grid.appendChild(agentDiv)` at line 133 but has no return statement and line 138 never reassigns `agentDiv`, so line 139 (`agentDiv.style.left = ...`) throws TypeError on null. The throw propagates out of the `serverAgents.forEach` callback (lines 59-63) inside the 'simulation_state_update' handler, skipping remaining agents and lines 64-67 (renderAgentSelectionPanel and inspector refresh) for that tick. The cadence claim is verified end-to-end: command.py:64 sets a 0.4s tick and line 71 emits 'simulation_state_update' each tick, app.py:58-61 rebroadcasts to browsers, and simulation/manager.py:349-353 includes all agents in every payload; with the fixed 6-agent roster (simulation/config.py:302-337) and stable dict iteration order, exactly one avatar is created per throwing tick, producing 6 uncaught exceptions per page load and ~2.4s before all avatars appear (roster on the first clean tick after). Only trivial imprecisions exist: the roster appears at tick N+1 rather than N, and the 'new agent mid-run' recurrence is hypothetical since the backend never adds agents after initialization (though every page reload/reconnect does reproduce the N throws). Neither misstates the mechanism or severity; the suggested fix is correct.

findings.title: Full DOM rebuild every 0.4s tick: roster clicks are swallowed and needs-bar animations defeated
findings.description: Every 'simulation_state_update' (each 0.4s tick from command.py:71-72) calls renderAgentSelectionPanel() (script.js:64), which does dom.roster.innerHTML='' and recreates all roster buttons (script.js:240-252). A button destroyed between the user's mousedown and mouseup never fires its click event, so selecting an agent from the roster intermittently does nothing (nodes are replaced ~every 0.4s). When an agent is selected, inspectAgent() also runs every tick (script.js:65-67), rebuilding inspector innerHTML, all needs bars, and re-joining the agent's entire 50-entry log via renderLog (script.js:203-205) — the needs-bar 'transition: width 0.3s' (style.css:190-194) never animates because the bars are recreated rather than updated, and the log/inspector DOM churns 2.5x/second.
findings.fix: Rebuild the roster only when the agent set changes (compare ids); update existing needs-bar widths, goal text, and log via targeted mutations (element.style.width, textContent, appending only new log entries) instead of innerHTML wipes.

verdict.justification: Every mechanism in the claim is verified by the code. command.py:64-72 emits 'simulation_state_update' every 0.4s while unpaused (manager.py:349-353,368 always returns a truthy state_payload, so the emit fires every tick), and app.py:58-61 rebroadcasts it to the browser. In static/script.js the handler (lines 46-68) calls renderAgentSelectionPanel() at line 64, which at lines 240-252 executes dom.roster.innerHTML='' and recreates all buttons with per-element onclick (line 249) and no event delegation — so a button replaced between mousedown and mouseup never fires its click, making roster selection intermittently fail (~100ms click window vs 400ms rebuild cycle). When an agent is selected, lines 65-67 rerun inspectAgent every tick, rebuilding inspector innerHTML (lines 153-162), recreating all needs bars (lines 157-162), and rejoining the full log via renderLog's innerHTML wipe (lines 203-205); entities.py:62-65 confirms the log caps at exactly 50 entries. style.css:190-194 defines transition: width 0.3s ease-in-out on .needs-bar, which never animates because each bar is a freshly inserted element with a static inline width rather than a mutated one. Refutation attempts failed: the pause guard (script.js:47) only suppresses updates while paused; map-avatar clicks work (avatars are mutated, not recreated, script.js:136-144) but are merely an alternative path, not a fix; and the separate updateAgentAvatar null-deref bug (script.js:137-139) only aborts the handler for the first few ticks until all avatars exist, after which the per-tick rebuild proceeds exactly as described. All cited line numbers are accurate and Major severity is appropriate for an intermittently broken primary interaction plus structurally defeated animations and constant 2.5x/sec DOM churn.

findings.title: README describes a py_trees architecture (QueryRAG/FollowPath/PickUpItem) that does not exist in the code
findings.description: README.md:152-154 states the BT 'is composed of several custom behavior nodes, such as QueryRAG, FollowPath, and ExploreAction, all of which inherit from py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour', that 'PickUpItem handles ... an agent acquiring an item', and that the root Selector prioritizes 'Deliver'/'PickUp' sequences based on has_item. The real implementation is a custom Node/Selector/Sequence/StatefulSelector framework (behavior/behavior_tree.py:37-196) with nodes like IsNeedCritical, ExecuteActivity, PlanPathToHome. Related inaccuracies: README.md:140 says the loop is 'managed by the Manager class' and its 'run_simulation method' — the class is AgentManager with a tick() method (manager.py:41,163), and run_simulation lives in command.py:47; README.md:146 cites behavioral flags 'like has_item' that Agent (entities.py) does not have; the clone URL at README.md:83 is a placeholder pointing at 'yourusername/Final-Project.git'.
findings.fix: Rewrite the 'Behavioral Control' section to describe the actual custom BT framework and node set, correct Manager->AgentManager and run_simulation->tick, drop has_item, and fix the clone URL.

verdict.justification: Every claim checks out against the source. (1) README.md:152 states the BT nodes "QueryRAG, FollowPath, and ExploreAction, all of which inherit from py_trees.behaviour.Behaviour" and that "PickUpItem handles the logical state change of an agent acquiring an item"; README.md:154 describes a root Selector prioritizing Deliver/PickUp sequences by item possession. Notably docs/v2_upgrade/drafts/stack_and_academic.md:14 admits "The README already cites it [py_trees]; V2 makes that true," corroborating that the README claim is currently false. (2) The actual implementation is a custom framework: behavior/behavior_tree.py:37 defines a plain `class Node` base (tick raises NotImplementedError — no py_trees inheritance), with Selector (:62), StatefulSelector (:83), Sequence (:157); real leaf nodes in behavior/agent_behaviors.py are IsNeedCritical (:10), ExecuteActivity (:178), PlanPathToHome (:428), etc., exactly as the finding says. (3) README.md:140 credits "the Manager class" and its "run_simulation method" for the loop — the class is AgentManager (simulation/manager.py:41) whose per-tick method is tick() (manager.py:163); run_simulation() is a module-level function in command.py:47 whose while-loop calls manager.tick() (command.py:66-69). (4) README.md:146 cites "key behavioral flags like has_item," but Agent.__init__ (simulation/entities.py:12-53) defines no has_item attribute. The description does not overstate mechanism or severity: within a quality/packaging audit, a README whose core architecture section describes an entirely nonexistent implementation (library, node names, agent flags, class/method names, clone URL) is a Major documentation defect that misleads anyone reading or extending the project.

findings.title: No dependency manifest, lockfile, tests, or CI anywhere in the repo
findings.description: Repo root contains no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py/setup.cfg, Pipfile, poetry.lock, or uv.lock (verified by listing the root and globbing). There is no tests/ directory, no test file anywhere, and no .github/ CI config. The only dependency record is the incomplete prose pip command in README.md:87-92 (see F06) and the analyzer docstring (narrative_analyzer.py:25-26). No Python version is declared (local __pycache__ shows cpython-313). With zero pins, environment reconstruction is guesswork — e.g. narrative_analyzer.py:189 hard-codes the matplotlib style name 'seaborn-v0_8' which only exists in matplotlib >= 3.6, so an unpinned older matplotlib crashes the analyzer in __init__. BT semantics, scheduling windows, pathfinding, and memory filtering are all untested — several of the bugs in this audit (e.g. F05, F17, F18) would be caught by basic unit tests.
findings.fix: Add a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml with pinned versions covering flask, flask-socketio, python-socketio[client], requests, python-dotenv, and the analysis stack; declare requires-python; add a pytest suite (BT node contract tests, schedule-window property tests, BFS tests, memory-filter tests, smoke test running N ticks with a mock LLM) and a CI workflow that installs from the manifest and runs it.

(2) No tests: glob **/*test* returned nothing, and `git ls-files | grep -iE 'requirements|pyproject|setup|Pipfile|lock|test|github|yml|yaml'` matched zero tracked files. (3) No CI: `.github/` does not exist (`test -d .github` fails) and no workflow/yml files are tracked. (4) The only dependency records are the prose pip commands at README.md:88-91 (`pip install flask flask-socketio python-dotenv` / `pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn textblob networkx numpy`) and the docstring list at narrative_analyzer.py:25-26 ("Requirements: pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, textblob, networkx, numpy") — and that README list is indeed incomplete, since command.py:5 imports `socketio` (python-socketio client, whose connect path needs the [client] extras) and simulation/llm_handler.py:4 imports `requests`, neither of which is listed. (5) The matplotlib version-sensitivity example is accurate: narrative_analyzer.py:189 executes `plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8')` inside NarrativeAnalyzer.__init__ (def at line 170); the 'seaborn-v0_8' style name was only introduced in matplotlib 3.6 (older versions ship the style as 'seaborn'), so an unpinned matplotlib < 3.6 raises OSError in __init__ before any analysis runs. (6) No Python version is declared anywhere, and __pycache__/app.cpython-313.pyc confirms the local interpreter is CPython 3.13 as the finding states. The one soft claim — that bugs F05/F17/F18 would have been caught by basic unit tests — is an opinion about testability rather than a checkable code behavior, but it does not misstate any mechanism. Severity Major is appropriate for a packaging/quality audit: environment reconstruction for a multi-process (server + client + analyzer) Python project is pure guesswork, with at least one demonstrated version-dependent crash path.

findings.title: BFS uses list.pop(0) with full-path copies, and returned paths start with the agent's own cell — one wasted movement tick per trip
findings.description: find_path_bfs uses a plain list as the queue with queue.pop(0) (O(n) per dequeue, manager.py:29) and stores a full copied path per enqueued node (new_path = list(path), manager.py:36-37), giving roughly O(V^2) time/memory on the 30x23 grid — run per agent per (re)plan, plus a fresh occupied_for_pathing set comprehension per agent per tick (manager.py:243, 287, 307). Correctness quirks: the returned path includes the start cell as path[0] and path_index starts at 0 (manager.py:271-272), so the first 'move' (manager.py:284-285, 324-325) steps the agent onto its own current cell — every journey loses one tick (2 sim-minutes). Also, is_traversable's target short-circuit (manager.py:22-23) is evaluated after the wall check but before the occupied check, so BFS will path onto an occupied target cell when a caller passes one (e.g. the _get_agent_home_target all-occupied fallback at manager.py:159-161), which then permanently trips the blocked check on the final step. Fine for 6 agents, but wasteful and quietly wrong.
findings.fix: Use collections.deque with popleft(), store parent pointers and reconstruct the path once, drop the start cell (or start path_index at 1), and treat an occupied target as unreachable (or pick a new target); optionally cache paths or switch to A*.

verdict.justification: All cited mechanics verified in simulation/manager.py. find_path_bfs uses a plain list with queue.pop(0) (line 29, O(n) dequeue) and copies the full path per enqueued node (lines 36-37). The queue is seeded with [((start),[ (start) ])] (line 15) so the returned path includes the start cell as path[0]; callers set path_index=0 (lines 271-272, 311-312), and the movement code (285, 324-325) assigns the agent to path[0] — its own cell — consuming one movement tick per planned trip (grid confirmed 30 cols x 23 rows from static/map_data.json). is_traversable returns True for the target cell (lines 22-23) before the occupied check (lines 24-25), so BFS will path onto an occupied target; _get_agent_home_target's all-occupied fallback (lines 159-161) returns the raw home cell which can be occupied, after which the final step trips the blocked check at line 288 for as long as the occupant remains. Fresh occupied-position set comprehensions are rebuilt at lines 243, 287 (named current_occupants), and 307. Only trivial nits: line 287's variable is current_occupants not occupied_for_pathing, and 'permanently' holds only while the occupying agent stays put — neither changes the substance.

findings.title: Priority inversion in the root Selector: 'Urgent: Rest' (energy>=70) outranks 'Critical: Find Food' (hunger>=85), so tired-and-starving agents never eat
findings.description: Root children order (lines 608-632): emergency home (energy>=95), rest (energy>=70), food (hunger>=85), then the schedule. Since the rest sequence returns SUCCESS every tick it plans a path (and livelocks per F11), an agent whose energy is >=70 never evaluates the food branch even at hunger 100 — the comments themselves label food 'Critical' and rest 'Urgent', so the ordering contradicts the stated intent. During the rest/emergency pacing livelocks, hunger rises 0.25/tick (entities.py:74,82) and pins at 100 with no recovery path.
findings.fix: Reorder the root children so the starvation branch precedes the tiredness branch (or gate rest on hunger < 85), keeping the energy>=95 emergency above both only if it gains a real sleep action (F12).

verdict.justification: behavior/agent_behaviors.py lines 608-632: the root is a stateless Selector (behavior_tree.py lines 62-76, re-evaluates from the first child and short-circuits on any non-FAILURE) ordered emergency-home (IsAgentTired threshold=95, line 611), rest (IsAgentTired threshold=70, line 616), food (IsNeedCritical hunger threshold=85, line 626), then schedule. When energy>=70 the rest sequence never returns FAILURE: PlanPathToRestLocation unconditionally returns SUCCESS (line 465) and ExecuteRest returns RUNNING (line 490), so the food branch is provably never evaluated while energy>=70, even at hunger 100. The names/comments confirm the inverted intent: 'Critical: Find Food When Starving' (line 625) sits below 'Urgent: Rest when tired' (line 615). Hunger rises 0.25/tick when awake (entities.py lines 74, 82) with min(100,...) pinning, and the eat paths (ExecuteEat, scheduled lunch/dinner via the core branch) are all below the rest branch in the selector, so no hunger recovery is reachable while the condition holds. One caveat that keeps this Minor rather than worse: ExecuteRest drops energy by 70 on its first executed tick (line 485), so agents that actually reach rest execution escape the inversion; the pinned-at-100 outcome requires the rest branch to keep re-planning (the referenced F11 livelock), which the finding states as its premise.

findings.title: Wage rates are applied per tick but documented per hour (30x discrepancy), and tuning constants are scattered as magic numbers across five files
findings.description: manager.py:218-223 credits +0.8 ('Cafe workers earn more per hour'), +0.3, +0.5 per TICK while state=='doing_action'. A tick is 2 sim-minutes (manager.py:168), so the effective rates are $24/$9/$15 per sim-hour — 30x what the comments state — and job detection is string matching ('work'/'shift'/'classes' in the activity name, manager.py:206-208). More broadly, core tuning values are inline literals outside the designated config.py: time step 'minute += 2' (manager.py:168), story hour 3 (manager.py:356), per-personality sleep windows (manager.py:113-126), needs growth/decay rates (entities.py:74-78), starting money 100-150 (entities.py:39), log cap 50 (entities.py:64), tick interval 0.4s (command.py:64), interaction durations 15-25 and 8-15 (manager.py:338, agent_behaviors.py:221), rest/eat recovery -70 and thresholds 95/70/85 (agent_behaviors.py:485,535,611-626), and the socialize cutoff hour 22 duplicated in three places (manager.py:89, agent_behaviors.py:193). Tuning requires hunting through five files, paired values can silently drift, and the economy is impossible to reason about (interacting badly with F13's repeated charging).
findings.fix: Define named constants in simulation/config.py (e.g. TICK_MINUTES, STORY_HOUR, WAGE_PER_HOUR by role, NEED_RATES, SLEEP_WINDOWS) with units documented at the definition site, and compute per-tick pay from them.

verdict.justification: manager.py lines 218-223 credit +0.8/+0.3/+0.5 once per tick while state=='doing_action', with the comment 'Cafe workers earn more per hour' framing the values as hourly; a tick advances time by 2 sim-minutes (line 168), so 30 ticks/sim-hour makes the effective rates $24/$9/$15 per sim-hour — the 30x arithmetic checks out. Job detection is substring matching on 'work'/'shift'/'classes' (lines 206-208). Every cited magic number verified at its cited location: minute += 2 (manager.py:168), hour==3 story trigger (356), per-personality sleep windows (113-126), needs rates 0.25/0.15/0.1/0.2/0.8 (entities.py:74-78), starting money randint(100,150) (entities.py:39), log cap 50 (entities.py:64), tick interval 0.4 (command.py:64), interaction durations randint(15,25) (manager.py:338) and randint(8,15) (agent_behaviors.py:221), rest/eat recovery -70 (agent_behaviors.py:485, 535), thresholds 95/70/85 (611/616/626), and hour-22 cutoff duplicated in manager.py:89, agent_behaviors.py:193, and the (20,22) schedule entries in config.py. config.py exists as the designated config file yet holds none of these. Minor interpretive stretch: only the cafe comment says 'per hour' (the 0.3/0.5 comments don't state units), but the applied-per-tick vs hourly-documentation mismatch is real.

findings.title: State payload resends every agent's full 50-entry log 2.5 times per second, and the server echoes the whole payload back to the sender
findings.description: to_dict() (entities.py:103-120) includes the entire log list (up to 50 timestamped strings per agent, entities.py:64) in every 'simulation_state_update', built and emitted every 0.4s for all 6 agents (manager.py:349-353, command.py:69-71) even when nothing changed — ~300 log lines (tens of KB) resent 2.5x/second per client, though at most one new entry per agent can appear per tick; it grows linearly with agent count and forces the frontend's renderLog churn (F27). The server relay uses emit(..., broadcast=True) (app.py:58-61), which includes the sender, so the full payload is also echoed back to the command client (which has no handler for it) — roughly doubling wasted bandwidth.
findings.fix: Send logs incrementally (only entries added since the last tick, or an incrementing sequence number so clients request deltas; full log on demand when an agent is inspected), and relay with emit(..., broadcast=True, include_self=False) or socketio.emit(..., skip_sid=request.sid).

verdict.justification: entities.py to_dict (lines 103-120) includes the full 'log' list (line 117), which add_log caps at 50 entries (lines 62-65). manager.tick builds the payload with every agent's full dict unconditionally every tick (lines 349-353), and command.py emits it every 0.4s (simulation_tick_interval=0.4, line 64; emit at 69-71) — 2.5x/second — regardless of whether anything changed. AGENT_CONFIG has 6 agents (config.py:302-337), so up to ~300 timestamped strings per payload, growing linearly with agent count. The relay handler app.py:58-61 uses flask_socketio emit(..., broadcast=True) without include_self=False/skip_sid, which includes the sender, so the command client (which registers no 'simulation_state_update' handler — command.py has only connect/connect_error/disconnect/pause/resume) receives the full payload back. One immaterial inaccuracy in an aside: more than one log entry per agent can be added in a single tick (e.g., the StatefulSelector decision log at behavior_tree.py:109 plus a plan-path log in the same tick), but this doesn't affect the defect as described.

findings.title: No LLM output validation: truncated diaries and null content are silently accepted or crash downstream
findings.description: generate_narrative blindly returns response.json()['choices'][0]['message']['content'] with no schema check and no finish_reason inspection. The diary prompt demands entries 'as complete and long as possible' (narrative_system.py:35) against max_tokens=2048, so hitting the cap yields a diary truncated mid-sentence that is written to disk (narrative_system.py:41-42) and then fed verbatim into the town-story prompt (narrative_system.py:50-58) — garbage-in for the second LLM stage with no detection. If the API returns 200 with content=null (e.g. a content filter), `diary_entry + "\n"` at narrative_system.py:42 raises TypeError, which rides the crash path that kills the sim (F01).
findings.fix: Validate the response shape (use .get with explicit errors), assert content is a non-empty string, and check choices[0]['finish_reason']; on 'length', accept-and-log or retry with a tighter prompt. Raise a single well-typed LLMError the caller can catch.

verdict.justification: llm_handler.py generate_narrative (line 39) returns response.json()['choices'][0]['message']['content'] with no shape validation and no finish_reason inspection. The diary prompt demands the entry be 'as complete and long as possible' (narrative_system.py:35) with max_tokens=2048 (line 37), so a length-capped response yields a mid-sentence truncated diary that is written to disk at lines 41-42 and then read back verbatim into the town-story prompt (lines 50-58/56-65) with no detection. If the API returns 200 with content=null, `diary_entry + "\n"` at line 42 raises TypeError; write_agent_diary is called from manager.tick (manager.py:362), and the exception propagates to command.py's loop where `except Exception` at lines 76-78 prints and breaks — terminating the simulation.

findings.title: Prompts are raw string concatenation of prior LLM output and agent logs — brittle and injectable
findings.description: compile_daily_story concatenates all six diary entries (themselves unvalidated LLM output) with '---' separators and appends the instructions AFTER the untrusted text (narrative_system.py:56-65), all in a single user message with no system role and no delimiting. A diary that happens to contain instruction-shaped text (or a '---' line) can hijack or derail the town story. write_agent_diary similarly interpolates raw memory event strings as bullet lines (narrative_system.py:32); those strings embed volatile debug-ish content like behavior-tree scores ('(Score: 0.85)', behavior/behavior_tree.py:109) and pathfinding complaints ('My path to X is blocked', manager.py:289), which the prompt then asks the LLM to treat as the agent's lived experience.
findings.fix: Put instructions in a system message and wrap each diary/memory block in explicit delimiters (XML-ish tags or fenced blocks) with a note that the enclosed text is data, not instructions. Filter or rephrase mechanical log lines (scores, path errors) before they enter the diary prompt.

verdict.justification: compile_daily_story (narrative_system.py:56-65) concatenates all agent diaries — themselves unvalidated LLM output — joined by '\n---\n' with the instructions appended AFTER the untrusted text, and generate_narrative sends everything as a single user message with no system role (llm_handler.py:29) and no delimiting, so instruction-shaped diary text or embedded '---' lines can derail the second stage. write_agent_diary interpolates raw memory event strings as '- {m.event}' bullets (line 32); those memories come from add_log which mirrors every UI log line into the memory stream (entities.py:66-69), including mechanical lines like the StatefulSelector's 'I've decided to: ... (Score: {best_score:.2f})' (behavior_tree.py:109) and 'My path to {destination} is blocked, finding a new spot.' (manager.py:289), which the prompt then presents as the agent's lived experiences.

findings.title: get_embedding is dead code, the API key uses a generic 'API_KEY' env var with no fail-fast, and duplicate handler instances diverge
findings.description: A repo-wide grep for get_embedding matches only its definition (llm_handler.py:41-57); it is never called. The module and class docstrings claim 'narrative and embedding generation', but memory retrieval is a plain string-prefix filter on day names (memory.py:36-37) with no relevance ranking or semantic recall; the embedding endpoint config (llm_handler.py:19) and hardcoded legacy text-embedding-ada-002 model (llm_handler.py:48) are unreachable code that will bit-rot. The OpenAI key is read from a generic 'API_KEY' env var (llm_handler.py:16) rather than the conventional OPENAI_API_KEY, inviting collisions; if unset there is no error at construction — the Authorization header becomes literally 'Bearer None' and every call 401s. The startup check does catch that (command.py:51-58), but it costs a real completion call ('Say hello.') on every launch and validates a DIFFERENT LLMHandler instance than the one AgentManager builds for itself at manager.py:57, so the two can diverge if a key is passed explicitly to one.
findings.fix: Either delete get_embedding (and the embedding_url/docstring claims) or wire it into AgentMemoryStream for memory ranking with the same timeout/retry fixes. Read OPENAI_API_KEY with API_KEY as fallback and raise ValueError in __init__ when neither is set. Construct one LLMHandler in command.py, verify it, and pass it into AgentManager.

verdict.justification: Repo-wide grep for get_embedding matches only its definition (llm_handler.py:41-57); the only other hits are documentation drafts under docs/, not code — it is dead. The module and class docstrings (lines 2, 10) claim 'narrative and embedding generation', while actual memory retrieval is m.timestamp.startswith(day) (memory.py:36-37) with no ranking; embedding_url (line 19) and the hardcoded 'text-embedding-ada-002' (line 48) are unreachable. The key is read from os.getenv('API_KEY') (line 16) with no validation in __init__, so an unset key yields the literal header 'Bearer None' (f-string at lines 24/43/62) and API failures only at call time. The startup check (command.py:51-58) does catch this but sends a real 'Say hello.' completion (llm_handler.py:59-77) on every launch, and it validates a separate LLMHandler instance (command.py:51) from the one AgentManager constructs for itself (manager.py:57) — two independent instances that can diverge if a key is ever passed to one explicitly.

findings.title: Dead and vestigial code throughout: _pending_narrative flags never read, no-op reset_agent_diaries, unused returns, brittle hour==3 trigger, unused imports
findings.description: Verified dead paths: (1) manager.py:182-183 sets self._pending_narrative_day/_pending_narrative at day rollover, but nothing ever reads them (grep-verified) and they are never initialized in __init__ — an abandoned deferred-narrative mechanism; the live trigger is instead the literal `hour == 3 and minute == 0` check (manager.py:356), which only fires because the +2-minute increment (manager.py:168) happens to divide 60 — changing the tick granularity would silently disable all narrative generation. (2) NarrativeSystem.reset_agent_diaries (narrative_system.py:72-75) is a documented no-op 'pass' still invoked each night from manager.py:365, giving the false impression per-day cleanup happens. (3) tick() returns an always-empty commands list (manager.py:368) that command.py:69 discards. (4) self.daily_stories (manager.py:59, 364) is appended daily but never read by anything in either process — no way for late-joining browsers to fetch past stories. (5) The random.shuffle before day-rollover BT resets (manager.py:176-179) has no effect. (6) Unused imports: config.py:5 'random'; narrative_system.py:5-7 'datetime', 'shutil', 'LLMHandler'; narrative_analyzer.py 'json', 'Any', 'Counter', 'patches', 'ConnectionPatch'; narrative_analyzer.py:709/724 builds routine_patterns but never reads it.
findings.fix: Delete the dead attributes, no-op method and call site, unused returns, pointless shuffle, and unused imports — or make _pending_narrative the actual narrative trigger so generation is robust to tick-size changes; serve daily_stories via an HTTP route/socket replay or remove the list. Run ruff/flake8 (F401/F841) in CI to keep dead code out.

verdict.justification: Every enumerated item verified. (1) self._pending_narrative_day/_pending_narrative are assigned at manager.py:182-183, never initialized in __init__, and a repo-wide grep finds no other reference; the live trigger is the literal `hour == 3 and minute == 0` at line 356, which only fires because the +2 increment (line 168) divides 60 so minute==0 recurs each hour. (2) reset_agent_diaries is a documented no-op `pass` (narrative_system.py:72-75) still called nightly at manager.py:365. (3) tick() returns `[], state_payload` (line 368) and command.py:69 unpacks and never uses the commands list. (4) self.daily_stories (manager.py:59, appended at 364) is never read — narrative_analyzer.py's daily_stories is a separate attribute loaded from disk files, and app.py exposes no route to replay past stories to late-joining clients. (5) random.shuffle at line 177 precedes per-agent BT resets that are order-independent, so it has no effect. (6) Unused imports confirmed by grep: config.py:5 'random' (no other occurrence in the file); narrative_system.py lines 5-7 'datetime', 'shutil', 'LLMHandler' (none referenced in the 75-line file); narrative_analyzer.py 'json' (no json. usage), 'Any', 'Counter', 'ConnectionPatch' (import lines only), and the 'patches' alias (no patches. usage); routine_patterns is built at narrative_analyzer.py:709 and written at 724 but only the parallel routine_data list is ever read (DataFrame at 737).

findings.title: Personality trait dict merge silently overwrites conflicting keys, and 16 of 19 trait keys are never read
findings.description: entities.py:23 merges traits with `{k: v for p in personality for k, v in PERSONALITY_TRAITS.get(p, {}).items()}` — later traits silently overwrite earlier ones on key collisions (e.g. an agent given both 'conscientious' (planning_focus 0.8) and 'spontaneous' (planning_focus 0.2) gets 0.2 with no warning), and unknown trait names are silently dropped via .get(p, {}). No current AGENT_CONFIG combo collides, so the hazard is latent. Additionally, of all keys defined in PERSONALITY_TRAITS (config.py:13-24) only 'talkativeness' (agent_behaviors.py:116), 'social_motivation' (entities.py:85), and 'work_ethic' (entities.py:96) are ever consumed; prefers_group, cooperativeness, conflict_aversion, planning_focus, exploration_tendency, learning_focus, routine_adherence, gym_motivation, health_focus, work_motivation, overtime_tendency, sleep_motivation, procrastination, party_motivation, and networking are decorative despite the comment 'influencing behavior tree decisions' (config.py:12).
findings.fix: Detect collisions in the merge (warn, or combine numerically via mean/max), raise on unknown trait names, and either wire the unused traits into the BT heuristics or trim them.

verdict.justification: Core defect fully verified: entities.py:23 contains the exact merge comprehension; later traits silently overwrite earlier on key collisions (conscientious planning_focus 0.8 vs spontaneous planning_focus 0.2 -> 0.2 wins, verified by dict-comprehension order) and unknown trait names are silently dropped via .get(p, {}). Programmatic check confirms no current AGENT_CONFIG combo collides (all 6 agents collision-free), so the hazard is latent as claimed. Grep confirms exactly 3 trait keys are ever consumed: talkativeness (agent_behaviors.py:116), social_motivation (entities.py:85), work_ethic (entities.py:96), and the 15 unused keys enumerated in the description are exactly correct. However the title's count is wrong: PERSONALITY_TRAITS defines 18 distinct keys of which 15 are unread (verified programmatically), not '16 of 19'. The description's own enumeration (15 unused + 3 used = 18) contradicts the title.

findings.title: 15+ ACTIVITY_DATA entries are unreachable dead config — the sim's behavioral repertoire is materially overstated
