findings.title: Home-coordinate mapping duplicated with magic ranges in two modules — drift makes 'am I home?' and home-target selection disagree
findings.description: IsAtActivityLocation._get_agent_home_locations (behavior/agent_behaviors.py:89-104) and AgentManager._get_agent_home_target (simulation/manager.py:138-153) contain the identical hardcoded region classification: home_x <= 5 and home_y <= 5 -> north_houses; home_x <= 5 and 13 <= home_y <= 17 -> central_houses; home_x <= 5 and home_y >= 18 -> south_houses; home_x >= 18 and home_y <= 5 -> student_accommodation. These magic ranges re-encode geometry that already lives in static/map_data.json 'places' coords, so any map or home_pos change (config.py:302-341) must be synchronized across three artifacts; if the two copies drift, the BT's home check and the manager's home-target selection disagree and agents oscillate.
findings.fix: Give each agent a home place reference in AGENT_CONFIG (or map home_pos to the place whose coords contain/neighbor it) and resolve it in one shared function called from both sites.

verdict.justification: IsAtActivityLocation._get_agent_home_locations (agent_behaviors.py:89-104) and AgentManager._get_agent_home_target (manager.py:138-153) contain literally identical region-classification conditionals (home_x<=5 and home_y<=5 -> north_houses; home_x<=5 and 13<=home_y<=17 -> central_houses; home_x<=5 and home_y>=18 -> south_houses; home_x>=18 and home_y<=5 -> student_accommodation; else exact-position fallback). static/map_data.json:42-44,53 confirms these ranges re-encode the places' coords (north_houses x2-4/y2-4, central_houses y14-16, south_houses y18-20, student_accommodation x18-20/y2-4), and home_pos values live in AGENT_CONFIG at config.py:302-341 — three artifacts that must stay synchronized. The oscillation consequence is stated conditionally ('if the two copies drift') and is a fair characterization since one function gates 'am I home' and the other picks the home target.

findings.title: Fixed 0.4s sleep with variable tick cost — simulated time drifts against wall clock
findings.description: time.sleep(0.4) after a tick whose duration varies (command.py:64, 72) yields no fixed-timestep accounting: the sim-time-to-real-time ratio is not stable, and it silently drifts with tick cost — most dramatically during the 03:00 LLM block (F03) when the '0.4s cadence' becomes minutes per tick.
findings.fix: Use a fixed-timestep loop with an accumulator, or schedule the next tick by deadline (sleep until start_time + n*interval) rather than sleeping a constant after variable work.

verdict.justification: command.py:64 sets simulation_tick_interval = 0.4 and line 72 executes time.sleep(simulation_tick_interval) after manager.tick(), with no accumulator or deadline-based scheduling — each tick advances sim time by a fixed 2 minutes (manager.py:168) regardless of how long the tick took, so the sim-to-real ratio drifts with tick cost. The 03:00 case is real: at hour==3, minute==0 manager.tick (manager.py:356-366) synchronously runs 6 write_agent_diary LLM calls plus 1 compile_daily_story call via requests.post with no timeout (llm_handler.py:33), so that tick can take minutes while still representing 2 simulated minutes.

findings.title: print()-based diagnostics throughout, no structured/replayable log, and split-brain type-hint standards
findings.description: All runtime diagnostics are bare print() statements across app.py:46/51, command.py:19-89, manager.py:77/180, llm_handler.py:37/55/76, and ~40 prints in narrative_analyzer.py — no levels, timestamps, or files, so long-running sims (the committed data spans 14 simulated days) have no persistent, filterable record; e.g. the OpenAI error print at llm_handler.py:37 is lost in tick spam, and there is no structured event journal from which a run could be reconstructed or replayed. Style is also split-brain: narrative_analyzer.py is fully type-hinted with rich docstrings, while the entire simulation/ and behavior/ packages have zero type hints (manager.tick, Agent.__init__, all BT nodes), making the core simulation the least self-documented part of the codebase.
findings.fix: Introduce the logging module (or structlog) with a shared config (console + rotating file, JSON output) and replace prints; add an append-only event journal for replay; add type hints to the public surfaces of simulation/ and behavior/ to match the analyzer's standard.

verdict.justification: All diagnostics are bare print() with no logging module anywhere in code (grep for logging/structlog/getLogger matches only docs/ drafts): app.py:46/51 (2 prints), command.py 15 prints within lines 19-89, manager.py:77/180 (2), llm_handler.py:37/55/76 (3, including the OpenAI error print at :37), and narrative_analyzer.py has 57 prints (even more than the '~40' claimed). Committed narrative data spans day_1 through day_14 folders — 14 simulated days — with no structured/replayable journal. The type-hint split is real: narrative_analyzer.py imports typing and annotates its functions with rich docstrings, while grep finds zero type-hint syntax in simulation/ and behavior/ (manager.tick, Agent.__init__, and all BT nodes are unannotated).

findings.title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY, CORS wildcard, debug=True with allow_unsafe_werkzeug, and module-level file I/O
findings.description: app.py:11 hardcodes app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'a_new_secret_key_for_the_refactor' in source control; app.py:12 sets cors_allowed_origins='*' so any origin can connect to the SocketIO server and inject events — the handlers at lines 58-71 blindly rebroadcast whatever they receive, so any web page a user visits could spoof sim state or pause the engine; app.py:74 runs socketio.run(debug=True, allow_unsafe_werkzeug=True) — the Werkzeug interactive debugger allows arbitrary code execution if the port is ever reachable by anyone else, and allow_unsafe_werkzeug explicitly overrides Flask-SocketIO's production guard while debug's reloader double-runs the module-level map loading. map_data.json is also read at import time (app.py:17-26), so importing app in any process performs file I/O and dictates cwd assumptions. Acceptable for a localhost demo, but these are checked-in defaults with no env-var override despite the project already using python-dotenv.
findings.fix: Load SECRET_KEY from the environment (os.getenv with a random fallback), restrict cors_allowed_origins to the served origin (http://localhost:5000 / http://127.0.0.1:5000, or omit since the page is same-origin), gate debug/allow_unsafe_werkzeug behind an env flag, and lazy-load map data.

verdict.justification: All cited facts verified: app.py:11 hardcodes SECRET_KEY = 'a_new_secret_key_for_the_refactor'; :12 sets cors_allowed_origins='*'; the handlers at :58-71 (simulation_state_update, pause_simulation, resume_simulation) rebroadcast received data verbatim with broadcast=True, and command.py:32-44 honors relayed pause_simulation events, so any origin's page can pause the engine or spoof state; :74 runs socketio.run(app, debug=True, allow_unsafe_werkzeug=True) — debug=True enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger and its reloader, whose child-process re-import double-runs the module-level map load; map_data.json is read at import time at :17-26. The project already uses python-dotenv (llm_handler.py:5,15) yet none of these settings have env-var overrides.

findings.title: LLM and simulation text injected via innerHTML — latent stored XSS
findings.description:
LLM-generated story text is interpolated raw into innerHTML at script.js:89 (renderFullDailyStories: '${story.day}...${story.text}') and again in the dead renderDailyStoryPanel at line 260. Agent-derived strings also flow through innerHTML sinks: current_action/money/personality and current_goal (script.js:154-155), needs keys (160), log entries via logToMain/renderLog (195, 204 — logArray.join('
') includes server-relayed agent log strings), and roster names (248). Today the story panel never receives data (F04) and agent strings originate from config/simulation code, so exploitation requires the LLM to emit markup — but model output is uncontrolled: a story containing '' would execute in every viewer's browser the moment the daily-story event is wired up. This is the exact sink the architecture will feed with model output.
findings.fix: Use textContent (or a small escapeHTML helper applied to every interpolated value) when rendering story text, goals, actions, log entries, and names; reserve innerHTML for the static markup skeleton only.

verdict.justification:
Every cited sink verified at the exact lines: script.js:89 interpolates story.day and story.text (LLM-generated, delivered via the 'new_daily_story' socket event at :95-101) raw into li.innerHTML; the same pattern repeats at :260 in renderDailyStoryPanel, which is dead code (only caller addDailyStory is never invoked, and its target element lives in the #daily-story-panel removed at :71-72); :154-155 inject current_action/money/personality and current_goal via innerHTML; :160 interpolates needs keys into needsHTML assigned to innerHTML at :162; logToMain (:195) and renderLog (:204, logArray.join('
') into dom.log.innerHTML) render server-relayed agent log strings including renderLog(agent.log) at :165; :248 injects agent icon/name into btn.innerHTML. Currently agent strings originate from config/simulation code and the daily-story event never reaches the browser (emit_daily_story fires on the non-serving SocketIO instance in the command.py process), so it is accurately characterized as latent stored XSS whose trigger is uncontrolled model output.

findings.title: UI depends entirely on third-party CDNs — hard-fails offline and uses the Tailwind Play CDN in production
findings.description: index.html:14 loads the Tailwind Play CDN (explicitly not for production — runtime JIT compilation plus a console warning), line 15 loads Google Fonts, and line 18 pins socket.io client 4.0.1 from cdnjs (an early-2021 release, far behind the flask-socketio 5.x server's supported client line). With no internet (or a CDN outage/blocked network), the socket.io script fails to load, so `const socket = io()` at script.js:35 throws ReferenceError and the entire script dies — not even the locally served map (fetch('/map_data.json')) renders, despite the app otherwise being fully local. All styling also disappears since most classes are Tailwind utilities.
findings.fix: Vendor the socket.io client into static/ (or serve it from the flask-socketio package), replace the Tailwind Play CDN with a pre-built CSS file (tailwindcss CLI build) or plain CSS, and self-host/fallback the font.

verdict.justification: Core claims verified: index.html:14 loads the Tailwind Play CDN (cdn.tailwindcss.com, explicitly not for production), :15 loads Google Fonts, :18 pins socket.io client 4.0.1 from cdnjs (released March 2021; README's unpinned 'pip install flask flask-socketio' yields the 5.x server line today). The offline failure mode is provable: if the CDN script fails, top-level 'const socket = io()' at script.js:35 throws ReferenceError, execution aborts before 'window.onload = initialize' (:326) is assigned, so the locally served map (fetch('/map_data.json')) never renders. However, 'All styling also disappears' is overstated: the locally served static/style.css defines the core layout (#app-container, #game-area, grid cells and map colors, .agent-avatar, #ui-panel, .panel-section, needs bars), so only the Tailwind utility classes (typography, spacing, button/roster/needs-bar fill colors) are lost, not all styling.

findings.title: No disconnect/error states: the UI silently freezes when the sim client or server dies
findings.description: script.js registers only socket.on('connect') (line 38) and 'command_client_ready' (line 39). There is no handler for 'disconnect' or 'connect_error', and the server never signals when the command client drops (app.py has connect/disconnect prints at lines 43-51 but broadcasts nothing). If command.py crashes (which F01 makes likely) or app.py goes down, the browser keeps showing the last agent positions and a live-looking clock with no indication anything failed; the pause button remains clickable and emits into the void. isEngineReady is also never reset, so a restarted command client's state is not reflected.
findings.fix: Add socket.on('disconnect')/'connect_error' handlers that show a visible banner and disable controls; have app.py track the command client's sid and broadcast a 'command_client_disconnected' event so the UI can show 'simulation engine offline'.

verdict.justification: script.js registers only 'connect' (line 38), 'command_client_ready' (39), 'simulation_state_update' (46), and 'new_daily_story' (95); grep confirms no 'disconnect' or 'connect_error' handler anywhere in static/. app.py's disconnect handler (lines 48-51) only prints and broadcasts nothing, so browsers get no signal when command.py or the server dies. isEngineReady is set true at line 41 and never reset, and the pause button is enabled at line 43 and never re-disabled, so it stays clickable and emits into a dead session. Every specific claim matches the code.

findings.title: Pause state desyncs across browser clients — the server broadcasts pause/resume but the frontend never subscribes
findings.description: app.py deliberately rebroadcasts 'pause_simulation'/'resume_simulation' to all clients (app.py:63-71, broadcast=True), but script.js registers no listeners for either event — the pause button handler (script.js:272-285) only toggles local state optimistically. With two browsers open, tab A pausing the engine leaves tab B's isSimulationPaused=false and its button reading 'Pause Simulation'; tab B's next click emits a redundant pause while flipping its own label to 'Resume', and after tab A resumes, a tab that believes it is paused (with isEngineReady=true) drops incoming state updates at script.js:47. The single-client path works only because command.py stops emitting while paused.
findings.fix: Subscribe to 'pause_simulation'/'resume_simulation' in script.js and drive isSimulationPaused plus the button label/color from those server broadcasts instead of (or in addition to) local toggling.

verdict.justification: app.py:63-71 rebroadcasts 'pause_simulation'/'resume_simulation' with broadcast=True, but script.js has no socket.on listener for either event — the only pause logic is the local optimistic toggle in the button handler (272-285). The desync scenario traces exactly: tab B keeps isSimulationPaused=false after tab A pauses; tab B's click emits a redundant pause while flipping its label to 'Resume'; and a tab with isSimulationPaused=true and isEngineReady=true drops incoming updates at the line-47 guard. command.py:68 confirms the engine stops emitting while paused, which is why single-client use masks the bug.

findings.title: Dead UI code: static daily-story panel removed at runtime, unreachable/broken render functions, orphaned CSS, and advertised-but-missing interactions
findings.description: index.html:36-39 ships a #daily-story-panel that script.js:70-72 immediately removes on load, replacing it with a dynamically created #full-daily-story-panel (script.js:75-92). The leftover functions renderDailyStoryPanel and addDailyStory (script.js:254-268) are never called and reference the removed #daily-story-list — if ever invoked they would throw since getElementById returns null. style.css:196-238 styles elements that no longer exist, while the actual dynamic panel gets none of that styling. Also #game-grid-wrapper advertises 'cursor: grab' (style.css:53) and tabindex=0 (index.html:27) but no drag or keyboard handlers exist anywhere in script.js.
findings.fix: Delete the static panel from index.html, remove renderDailyStoryPanel/addDailyStory and the removal code, retarget the CSS to #full-daily-story-panel or delete it, and drop cursor:grab/tabindex or implement the implied drag-to-scroll.

verdict.justification: index.html:36-39 ships #daily-story-panel with #daily-story-list; script.js:71-72 removes it on load and renderFullDailyStories (75-92) creates #full-daily-story-panel instead. Grep confirms renderDailyStoryPanel/addDailyStory (254-268) are never called except by each other, and renderDailyStoryPanel would throw (getElementById('daily-story-list') returns null after removal, then .innerHTML on null). style.css:196-238 targets only the removed #daily-story-panel/#daily-story-list; #full-daily-story-panel appears nowhere in style.css. style.css:53 has cursor:grab and index.html:27 has tabindex="0", but the only addEventListener in static/ is the pause-button click — no drag or keyboard handlers exist.

findings.title: README claims a model-agnostic LLMHandler; the handler is hardcoded to OpenAI
findings.description: README.md:166 says 'the architecture of the LLMHandler is designed to be model-agnostic, allowing for the easy interchange of different language models.' In reality llm_handler.py:18-19 hardcodes https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions and /v1/embeddings, the request/response shapes are OpenAI-specific (response.json()['choices'][0]['message']['content'] at line 39), and the embedding model 'text-embedding-ada-002' is a literal at line 48. Only the chat model name is a constructor default ('gpt-4.1-mini', line 14) — no provider abstraction exists.
findings.fix: Either soften the README claim to 'OpenAI-compatible endpoint' or make base_url/embedding model configurable via env vars, which would also make the claim true for OpenAI-compatible local servers.

verdict.justification: README.md:166 contains the exact model-agnostic claim. simulation/llm_handler.py hardcodes https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions and /v1/embeddings at lines 18-19, parses the OpenAI-specific response.json()['choices'][0]['message']['content'] at line 39, and hardcodes 'text-embedding-ada-002' at line 48; only the chat model name is a constructor default ('gpt-4.1-mini', line 14). There is no base-URL, provider, or embedding-model configurability — no abstraction exists. (Finding's file field omits the simulation/ prefix, but all cited line numbers match the actual file.)

findings.title: Analyzer duplicates the agent roster and weekday mapping instead of importing simulation config
findings.description: AnalysisConfig hardcodes agents ['alex','bella','charlie','diana','ethan','fiona'] (narrative_analyzer.py:103) and day_names Monday..Sunday (lines 105-106), duplicating AGENT_CONFIG ids (simulation/config.py:300-343) and AgentManager.days (manager.py:49). load_simulation_data then derives filenames from '(day_num - 1) % 7' (line 241), silently assuming the simulation always starts on Monday (manager.py:52-53). Adding/renaming an agent in config.py, or changing the start day, makes the analyzer quietly load zero files for that agent (the per-file os.path.exists check at line 250 just skips them) and its stats no longer cover the simulation.
findings.fix: Import the roster from simulation.config (ids from AGENT_CONFIG) and discover day-of-week from the actual filenames in each day_N directory (e.g. glob '*_story.txt') rather than recomputing it from a duplicated Monday-start assumption.

verdict.justification: narrative_analyzer.py:103 hardcodes the six agent ids and lines 105-106 hardcode Monday-Sunday, duplicating AGENT_CONFIG (simulation/config.py:300-343) and AgentManager.days (simulation/manager.py:49, with Monday start via day_index=0 at lines 51-53). load_simulation_data derives filenames from day_names[(day_num-1)%7] at line 241 and the os.path.exists check at line 250 silently skips missing files (only a per-file warning on read errors, none for absence). A renamed/added agent or a non-Monday start would produce filenames the analyzer never looks for, silently loading zero files for that agent, exactly as claimed.

findings.title: Similarity heatmap rows sort lexicographically: day_10 renders before day_2, and weekdays sort alphabetically
findings.description: analyze_diary_story_similarity stores 'day' as the string key 'day_{N}_{Weekday}' (line 330) and _create_similarity_heatmap pivots on it (line 360: df.pivot(index='day', ...)). pandas sorts the pivot index lexicographically, so with the repo's 14 days the heatmap row order is day_1, day_10, day_11 ... day_14, day_2, day_3 ..., breaking the temporal reading of the visualization (the committed results/diary_story_similarity_heatmap.png is affected). The consistency heatmap (line 524, index='day_of_week') similarly orders weekdays alphabetically (Friday first) rather than Monday-Sunday.
findings.fix: Carry a numeric day column and reindex the pivot by it (sorted by day number); for day_of_week, reindex with self.config.day_names.

verdict.justification: The defect is real and verified empirically: df.pivot(index='day') on the committed diary_story_similarity.csv sorts lexicographically, and the committed results/diary_story_similarity_heatmap.png is affected (visually confirmed); the consistency pivot on 'day_of_week' (line 524) orders weekdays alphabetically Friday-first (also verified). However, the description misstates the actual row order: because the key is 'day_{N}_{Weekday}' and '_' sorts after digits, the real order is day_10..day_14 followed by day_1..day_9 — not 'day_1, day_10, ..., day_14, day_2, ...' as claimed. The headline ('day_10 renders before day_2') and the temporal-breakage conclusion are correct; only the stated sequence is wrong, so the finding is real but misdescribed in that detail.

findings.title: Keyword metrics use raw substring counting — 'work' matches 'workout', agent names match inside words, README stats are inflated
findings.description: All behavioral metrics use str.count on lowercased text: _analyze_behavioral_keywords (line 647), routine tracking (line 723: text.count(activity.lower())), and agent-mention networks (line 809: text.count(other_agent.lower())). With no word-boundary matching, 'work' (in work_behavior and activity_keywords) also counts every 'workout', 'working', 'homework', 'network'; 'usual' counts 'unusually'; overlapping keywords ('work' and 'gym', 'exercise' vs 'exercises') double-count. The README's quantitative results (e.g. 'Alex: 12.5 average work mentions', README.md:355) are systematically inflated, and fitness-oriented agents get spurious work_behavior credit for every workout mention.
findings.fix: Tokenize and match on word boundaries (e.g. len(re.findall(rf'\b{re.escape(kw)}\b', text))), and dedupe overlapping keyword sets before summing.

verdict.justification: All three cited sites use raw substring counting on lowercased text: text_lower.count(keyword) at line 647, text.count(activity.lower()) at line 723, and text.count(other_agent.lower()) at line 809, with 'work' present in both work_behavior (line 137) and activity_keywords (line 148) and 'usual' in routine_words (line 143). Empirically verified inflation: Alex's 14 diaries contain 90 substring matches for 'work' vs only 43 word-boundary matches, including 24 'workout' and 2 'working' hits — so the README's quantitative stats (README.md:355, 'Alex: 12.5 average work mentions' confirmed present) are systematically inflated by the mechanism exactly as claimed. Minor looseness in the 'work'/'gym' 'overlapping keywords' phrasing does not affect the core, provably true claim.

findings.title: Analyzer runtime is environment-fragile: CWD-relative paths, per-run NLTK downloads, version-pinned style string, global warning suppression
findings.description: Fragilities in NarrativeAnalyzer.__init__: (1) AnalysisConfig defaults stories_dir='simulation/narrative/daily_stories' and results_dir='results' (lines 96-97) as CWD-relative paths, so running 'python path/to/narrative_analyzer.py' from anywhere but the repo root raises FileNotFoundError (line 208) or scatters a results/ dir elsewhere; (2) setup_dependencies (lines 54-89, called at line 179) attempts five nltk.download calls on every run — requiring network access for a purely offline analysis and slowing startup (failures only warn, so offline first runs lose sentence tokenization silently); (3) plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8') (line 189) raises OSError on matplotlib < 3.6, a real failure mode with no pinned requirements; (4) warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') at line 51 globally suppresses all warnings, hiding real deprecations.
findings.fix: Anchor paths to os.path.dirname(__file__), check for NLTK data before downloading (nltk.data.find), wrap the style call in try/except with a fallback, and scope warning filters to the specific noisy categories.

verdict.justification: All four fragilities verified: (1) AnalysisConfig defaults stories_dir='simulation/narrative/daily_stories' and results_dir='results' at lines 96-97 are CWD-relative; __init__ does os.makedirs(results_dir) at line 182 and discover_available_days raises FileNotFoundError at lines 207-208 when run from another directory. (2) setup_dependencies (lines 54-89) attempts five nltk.download calls (line 66 lists 5 packages) on every construction (called at line 179), with failures only printing warnings (lines 71-72). (3) plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8') at line 189; the 'seaborn-v0_8' style names only exist in matplotlib >= 3.6, raising OSError on older versions, and the repo tracks no requirements.txt/pyproject/setup files (verified via git ls-files). (4) warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') at line 51 is a global, unscoped suppression.

related_work.name: Generative Agents (Smallville)
related_work.citation: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie Jun Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, and Michael S. Bernstein. 2023. Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior. In Proceedings of the 36th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '23), San Francisco, CA. ACM. DOI: 10.1145/3586183.3606763 (arXiv:2304.03442).
related_work.summary: Introduces an architecture where LLM-driven agents in a sandbox town maintain a natural-language memory stream with retrieval scored by recency/importance/relevance, synthesize higher-level reflections, and plan/react via LLM prompting; 25 agents produced emergent social behaviors like party organization and relationship formation. Evaluated with interview-based believability rankings by 100 human raters converted to TrueSkill ratings, plus ablations showing memory, reflection, and planning each matter.
related_work.difference_hook: The LLM sits inside every agent's perceive-plan-act loop, making behavior expensive, slow, and non-reproducible; it produces no external narrative artifacts (diaries or a town-wide story) from a verifiable event log. A BT+LLM hybrid keeps behavior deterministic, cheap, and re-runnable from a seed, and its LLM output can be audited sentence-by-sentence against symbolic ground-truth events.

related_work.name: Voyager
related_work.citation: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, and Anima Anandkumar. 2024. Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), March 2024 (arXiv:2305.16291, 2023). OpenReview: ehfRiF0R3a.
related_work.summary: The first LLM-powered lifelong-learning agent in Minecraft, combining an automatic curriculum, an ever-growing skill library of executable code, and iterative prompting with environment feedback and self-verification. It discovered 3.3x more unique items, traveled 2.3x farther, and unlocked tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior LLM-agent baselines.
related_work.difference_hook: Voyager is a single agent optimizing task competence (skill acquisition via code generation), not a multi-agent social simulation; it has no believability goals, no social memory, and generates no narrative artifacts. It also keeps GPT-4 in the action loop, whereas a BT hybrid confines the LLM to asynchronous post-hoc cognition.

related_work.name: AI Town (a16z)
related_work.citation: a16z-infra. 2023. AI Town: A MIT-licensed, deployable starter kit for a virtual town where AI characters live, chat and socialize. Open-source software, GitHub: a16z-infra/ai-town (TypeScript/Convex; ~10.1k stars).
related_work.summary: An engineering-focused open-source re-implementation of the Generative Agents concept as a deployable JS/TS starter kit, using Convex as the game engine/database, PixiJS rendering, and pluggable LLMs (Ollama, OpenAI, Together.ai) for character conversation and behavior. Explicitly inspired by Park et al. and aimed at making multiplayer-scalable LLM town simulations easy to fork.
related_work.difference_hook: AI Town is a software artifact, not a research contribution: it reports no evaluation, has no behavior-tree or utility-selection layer, no reflection loop, and does not distill event logs into diaries or a town chronicle. It is best cited as evidence of ecosystem demand rather than as a competing architecture.

related_work.name: Project Sid (Altera)
related_work.citation: Altera.AL: Andrew Ahn, Nic Becker, Stephanie Carroll, Nico Christie, Manuel Cortes, Arda Demirci, Melissa Du, Frankie Li, Shuying Luo, Peter Y. Wang, Mathew Willows, Feitong Yang, and Guangyu Robert Yang. 2024. Project Sid: Many-agent simulations toward AI civilization. arXiv:2411.00114 (submitted October 31, 2024).
related_work.summary: Simulates 10-1000+ LLM agents in Minecraft using the PIANO (Parallel Information Aggregation via Neural Orchestration) architecture, which runs concurrent cognitive modules while maintaining coherence across output streams for real-time interaction. Reports emergence of specialized roles, adherence to and amendment of collective rules (e.g., taxation), and propagation of cultural memes and religion, framed as 'civilizational benchmarks.'
related_work.difference_hook: PIANO parallelizes LLM cognition but keeps it in the control loop for every agent, incurring per-agent inference cost and non-determinism at scale; it measures civilizational progress, not narrative production. It has no symbolic BT substrate, no utility arbiter, and no mechanism for turning ground-truth logs into focalized per-agent diaries plus a global story.

related_work.name: AgentSociety
related_work.citation: Jinghua Piao, Yuwei Yan, Jun Zhang, Nian Li, Junbo Yan, Xiaochong Lan, et al. (Tsinghua University FIB Lab). 2025. AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society. arXiv:2502.08691. Open-source platform: github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/agentsociety.
related_work.summary: A large-scale social simulator combining LLM-driven agents endowed with theory-grounded 'minds' (emotions, needs, motivations) with a realistic urban environment engine, generating social lives for over 10,000 agents and ~5 million interactions. Used to study polarization, misinformation spread, and policy interventions (e.g., UBI), positioning simulation as a social-science instrument.
related_work.difference_hook: AgentSociety targets macro-social realism for social science, not game-AI believability or storytelling; validation is against aggregate real-world phenomena, not per-agent narrative coherence. It has no hybrid symbolic control layer and produces no literary artifacts from its logs.

related_work.name: GOAP / F.E.A.R. (classic planner hybrid)
related_work.citation: Jeff Orkin. 2006. Three States and a Plan: The A.I. of F.E.A.R. In Proceedings of the Game Developers Conference (GDC 2006), San Francisco. (Slides/paper via GDC Vault and gamedevs.org.)
related_work.summary: Canonical industry hybrid: a three-state FSM whose actions are sequenced at runtime by a STRIPS-style planner (GOAP) using A*, giving F.E.A.R.'s soldiers goal-directed squad behavior (suppression, flanking, environment use) without hand-authored mega-FSMs. It established the pattern of layering deliberative planning atop cheap reactive execution in shipped games.
related_work.difference_hook: GOAP plans over symbolic operators only: agents have no episodic memory, no natural-language cognition, and no capacity to narrate or reflect on their own history. A BT+LLM hybrid inherits GOAP's symbolic-control economics while adding language-based retrospective sense-making that classic planners cannot express.

related_work.name: ABL / Façade (believable-agent language + drama)
related_work.citation: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern. 2004. A Behavior Language: Joint Action and Behavioral Idioms. In H. Prendinger and M. Ishizuka (Eds.), Life-Like Characters: Tools, Affective Functions and Applications, Springer. See also: Mateas and Stern. 2005. Structuring Content in the Façade Interactive Drama Architecture. In Proc. AIIDE 2005, AAAI.
related_work.summary: ABL is a reactive-planning language (descended from Hap) for authoring believable agents with sequential, parallel, and joint behaviors; it implemented the character layer of Façade, the landmark interactive drama, whose beats were orchestrated by a drama manager. It remains the reference architecture for authored character believability in interactive narrative.
related_work.difference_hook: Every behavior and story beat in ABL/Façade is hand-authored at great expense; nothing is generated, and narrative does not emerge from simulation logs. The BT+LLM approach inverts this: cheap authored behavior generates events, and the narrative layer is synthesized post hoc rather than pre-scripted.

related_work.name: Utility AI (Dave Mark, IAUS)
related_work.citation: Dave Mark. 2009. Behavioral Mathematics for Game AI. Course Technology / Cengage Learning (Applied Mathematics series), ISBN 978-1584506843. See also: Mark et al., 'Architecture Tricks: Managing Behaviors in Time, Space, and Depth' (GDC AI Summit 2013, GDC Vault) and Mark & Lewis's Infinite Axis Utility System talks (GDC AI Summit 2015).
related_work.summary: Formalizes utility-based decision-making for game agents: response curves map world-state considerations to scores that are combined to select actions, culminating in the data-driven Infinite Axis Utility System (IAUS) deployed in shipped titles (e.g., at ArenaNet). It is the standard alternative/complement to BTs for context-sensitive action selection.
related_work.difference_hook: Utility AI selects among authored actions from numeric considerations but has no memory stream, no reflection, and no language faculty; scores are hand-tuned rather than derived from an agent's reflected experience. Using retrieval/reflection outputs to modulate utility-scored BT selection is precisely the coupling this literature lacks.

related_work.name: Hilburn's BT/planner hybrid
related_work.citation: Daniel Hilburn. 2013. Simulating Behavior Trees: A Behavior Tree/Planner Hybrid Approach. In Steve Rabin (Ed.), Game AI Pro: Collected Wisdom of Game AI Professionals, Chapter 8, pp. 99-111. CRC Press. (Verified via gameaipro.com chapter listing; also reprinted in Game AI Pro 360: Guide to Architecture, Routledge 2019.)
related_work.summary: Proposes simulating the forward execution of a behavior tree to obtain planner-like lookahead, combining BT authorability/reactivity with planning's ability to anticipate outcomes. Sits alongside sibling Game AI Pro chapters on BT starter kits (Champandard & Dunstan, ch. 6) and utility-in-BT integration (Merrill, ch. 10).
related_work.difference_hook: Hilburn's hybrid is entirely symbolic and forward-looking (predicting action outcomes); it has no backward-looking cognition. A BT+LLM narrative hybrid adds the retrospective direction — episodic memory, reflection, and story synthesis over what the BTs already did — which no BT/planner hybrid in the Game AI Pro line attempts. Note also Bill Merrill's 'Building Utility Decisions into Your Existing Behavior Tree' (Game AI Pro 2013, ch. 10) as prior art for utility-based BT selection specifically.

metrics.metric: Interview-based believability ranking with TrueSkill ratings
metrics.how_to_measure: Human evaluators watch agent 'interview' responses probing five capacities (self-knowledge, memory, plans, reactions, reflections) and rank architecture conditions by believability; rank data (Park et al.: 100 participants, 5 conditions) is converted to interval ratings via TrueSkill (Bayesian multiplayer Elo generalization), yielding a mean mu and sigma per condition (e.g., full architecture mu=29.89 vs. no-memory ablation mu=21.21).
metrics.used_by: Park et al., Generative Agents (UIST 2023) — the de facto standard believability protocol; directly reusable to compare BT-only vs. BT+memory vs. BT+memory+reflection conditions.

metrics.how_to_measure: Run the same simulation with memory retrieval, reflection, and (in our case) utility-based BT selection independently disabled, and compare believability/coherence scores across conditions; report per-component contribution as in Park et al.'s no-reflection / no-reflection-no-planning / no-memory ablations.
metrics.used_by: Park et al. (UIST 2023); also standard in Voyager's component ablations (curriculum, skill library, self-verification).

metrics.how_to_measure: Count distinct behaviors or outcomes over a fixed budget: Voyager measures unique items discovered (63 items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x baselines), map coverage / distance traveled (2.3x), and milestone unlock speed (tech-tree levels up to 15.3x faster in prompting iterations). Adapted to a town sim: distinct BT activations per agent-day, unique interaction pairs, entropy of daily activity distributions across agents and across seeded reruns.
metrics.used_by: Wang et al., Voyager (TMLR 2024); role-specialization emergence measures in Project Sid (arXiv:2411.00114).

metrics.how_to_measure: Track emergence of specialized roles, adherence to and amendment of collective rules, and propagation of cultural memes across the agent population over time, at increasing agent counts (Sid: 10-1000+ agents). For a town sim: measure relationship-graph growth, information diffusion (who learns of an event and when, verifiable from logs), and norm adoption rates.
metrics.used_by: Project Sid / Altera (2024) 'civilizational benchmarks'; AgentSociety (arXiv:2502.08691) validates against real-world macro phenomena (polarization, misinformation spread) at 10k+ agents / ~5M interactions.

metrics.metric: Narrative quality and factual grounding (hallucination rate against event log)
metrics.how_to_measure: Because the BT substrate emits a symbolic ground-truth event log, decompose each generated diary/story into atomic claims and label each as supported / unsupported / contradicted by the log — yielding a precision-style faithfulness score no pure-LLM simulation can compute; complement with human Likert or pairwise ratings of coherence, character consistency, and interestingness (and LLM-as-judge only as a secondary, bias-caveated signal).
metrics.used_by: The grounding audit is a novel opportunity of this architecture (no surveyed system does it); the human-rating protocol follows Park et al.'s rater methodology and standard story-generation evaluation practice.

metrics.how_to_measure: Report simulation throughput (ticks/sec or sim-time:real-time ratio) vs. agent count with LLM calls disabled and enabled; LLM tokens and dollar cost per simulated agent-day; and narrative-generation latency showing the async pipeline never blocks the simulation loop. Baseline comparison: Park et al. explicitly flag token cost as a limitation, and Project Sid's PIANO exists to manage real-time concurrency of in-loop LLM calls.
metrics.used_by: Project Sid (10-1000+ agent scaling); AgentSociety (10k-agent engine benchmarks); cost-as-limitation discussion in Park et al. (UIST 2023).

novelty_angles: Inverted control-flow hybrid: the LLM is removed from the per-tick decision loop entirely — deterministic, utility-selected behavior trees generate all behavior, and the LLM performs only post-hoc narrative cognition (per-agent diaries, town-wide chronicle) over the factual event log. No surveyed system (Generative Agents, AI Town, Project Sid, AgentSociety) separates behavior generation from language cognition this way; they all keep LLM inference in the action loop.

Verifiable narrative grounding as a first-class metric: because behavior is symbolic and fully logged, every generated sentence can be audited against ground-truth events, enabling a hallucination-rate/faithfulness score for emergent-narrative generation. Pure LLM-agent systems cannot compute this because their 'ground truth' (the memory stream) is itself LLM output.

Reflection-to-utility coupling: episodic retrieval and reflection outputs (Park et al.-style recency/importance/relevance scoring) parameterize a classical utility arbiter over behavior trees, rather than being spliced into prompts — connecting the Generative Agents cognitive loop to the Game AI Pro utility/BT tradition (Merrill 2013; Mark 2009) in a way neither literature has done.

Reproducibility and cost economics: seeded BT simulation reruns are bit-identical and near-free, with LLM cost amortized asynchronously and off the critical path — a direct answer to the cost/latency limitations Park et al. acknowledge and that PIANO (Project Sid) addresses only by parallelizing in-loop inference; this supports orders-of-magnitude more agent-hours per dollar and controlled A/B ablations.

Two-level focalized narration from one ground truth: the same event log is rendered both as first-person per-agent diaries and as an omniscient town chronicle, making narrative focalization/perspective over shared emergent events an object of study — absent from all surveyed systems, which either author narrative by hand (Facade) or don't produce narrative artifacts at all.

Honest non-novelty disclosure: BT/planner hybrids (Hilburn, Game AI Pro 2013), utility-driven BT selection (Merrill, Game AI Pro 2013), the memory-stream/reflection design itself (Park et al. 2023), retrieval-augmented agent memory (ICLR 2026 MemAgents workshop territory), and LLM diary/story generation in isolation are each established; the defensible claim is the specific composition, the grounding-auditable narrative pipeline, and the cost/believability evaluation of that composition — not any individual component.
